newsitem.title: USA: Report faults U.S. immigration procedures.
newsitem.headline: Report faults U.S. immigration procedures.

text.p: A review of 23 U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service offices found only one was in full compliance with procedures for checking citizenship applications, according to a report Friday.

The review was conducted by KPMG Peat Marwick LLP in February and March for the Justice Department, INS's parent agency, to see if the offices were following seven INS Naturalisation Quality Procedures issued last November.
Peat Marwick said it found the Boston District Office was meeting all the NQP requirements, seven other offices were in marginal compliance and the remaining 15 were noncompliant.

Many members of Congress have criticised the INS, saying the agency granted citizenship last year to thousands of unqualified aliens, including some with criminal records, because of poor background checks.
Over 1 million aliens were granted citizenship last year and some Republicans have charged applicants were rushed through so they could vote for Democrats in last November's elections.
INS Commissioner Doris Meissner has admitted errors were made because of a large backlog of applications and has promised to correct the problems. But she denies politics influenced INS actions.
The report said the biggest fault found was in checking criminal records and applicants' fingerprints with the FBI.

"As a result of our site reviews, it is now clear that the Naturalisation Quality Procedures has increased internal control and helped reduce the risk of incorrectly naturalising an applicant. But it is also clear the criminal history validation, a key control of the NQP, remains ineffective.

"Due to the inherent weaknesses in the FBI and INS matching, and the continued lack of control within the overall fingerprint process, we cannot provide assurance that INS is not continuing to incorrectly naturalise aliens with disqualifying conditions," the report said.
Representative Lamar Smith, a Texas Republican who chairs the House Immigration subcommittee, said of the findings: "Immediate action is required."
Smith said he would press Meissner to work out a plan to restore integrity to the naturalisation process immediately.
